name: MapReduce
statement: Process huge datasets in parallel by writing just two functions, a map and a reduce.
statementAccent: just two functions, a map and a reduce
meaning: MapReduce is a programming model, and an associated implementation, for processing and generating large data sets across a distributed cluster of many machines, in parallel. Its central idea is to let programmers express a computation as two simple functions and to have the framework handle the difficult parts of running it at scale, the parallelization, data distribution, fault tolerance, and load balancing, so the programmer can focus on the logic. The computation is written as two functions. The map function takes input key-value pairs and produces a set of intermediate key-value pairs. The reduce function merges, or aggregates, all the intermediate values associated with the same intermediate key. Between them sits a shuffle-and-sort step that groups all values by their intermediate key and routes them to the appropriate reducers. The classic example is counting words in a large collection of documents: the map function emits, for each word, the pair of that word and the count one, and the reduce function sums the counts for each word. MapReduce was developed at Google, and the paper MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters, by Jeffrey Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat, was published in 2004; it was inspired by, though it uses differently, the map and reduce functions of functional programming. The framework automatically handles machine failures by re-executing failed tasks and scales to thousands of commodity machines processing terabytes of data. It became hugely influential in big data, popularized broadly by the open-source Apache Hadoop, and later largely superseded for many workloads by systems such as Apache Spark.
mechanism: MapReduce structures a large-scale computation so that it can be automatically parallelized across a cluster, by forcing the programmer to express it in a restricted but powerful shape: a map followed by a reduce, with the framework orchestrating everything in between. The input data, typically enormous and split across many machines, is divided into pieces, and the framework runs a copy of the user's map function on each piece in parallel. Each map invocation reads input key-value pairs and emits intermediate key-value pairs; for word counting, it reads text and emits each word paired with the number one. The framework then performs the shuffle: it groups all intermediate pairs by key, so that every value produced for a given key, no matter which mapper produced it or on which machine, is collected together, and it sorts and routes these grouped values to the reduce workers. Each reduce invocation receives one intermediate key and the list of all values associated with it, and applies the user's reduce function to combine them into a smaller set of outputs; for word counting, it sums the ones to produce each word's total. The power of the model is that this map, shuffle, reduce skeleton is fixed, so the framework can supply all the hard distributed-systems machinery once and for all: it partitions the input, schedules tasks across machines, moves data, balances load, and, crucially, tolerates failures by detecting machines that die or stall and simply re-executing their tasks elsewhere, since the functions are deterministic and their inputs are preserved. This lets programmers with no expertise in parallel or distributed programming process terabytes across thousands of commodity machines. The model was inspired by the map and reduce combinators of functional languages, though the distributed, key-grouped reduce differs from their original meaning.

examples.text: Map emits each word paired with one; reduce sums the ones to give each word's total count.
The framework groups all intermediate values by key and routes them to the reducers between map and reduce.
The framework detects failed machines and re-executes their tasks, since the functions are deterministic.

whyItMatters: MapReduce is one of the most influential ideas in the history of large-scale computing, the model that made it practical for ordinary programmers to process web-scale datasets across thousands of machines, and it launched the modern big-data era. Before MapReduce, harnessing a large cluster meant grappling directly with the notorious hazards of distributed programming, partitioning data, coordinating machines, balancing load, and recovering from the constant failures that occur at scale, work so difficult that only specialists could attempt it. MapReduce's breakthrough was to hide all of that behind a simple interface: express the computation as a map and a reduce, and the framework takes care of the rest, automatically parallelizing the work, distributing the data, and re-executing tasks when machines fail. This let Google, and then the wider world, process terabytes and petabytes routinely, powering search indexing, log analysis, machine learning data preparation, and countless other tasks. The 2004 paper by Dean and Ghemawat inspired the open-source Apache Hadoop, which brought MapReduce and its distributed filesystem to everyone and created an entire big-data industry and ecosystem. Even though later systems like Apache Spark, which keep data in memory and offer richer operations, have superseded MapReduce for many workloads, and Google itself moved on, MapReduce established the paradigm of expressing big-data computation as functional transformations run in parallel over a cluster. As the model that processes huge datasets through just a map and a reduce, MapReduce reshaped computing at scale.

working.text: run the map function on each piece of the input to emit intermediate key-value pairs.
group all intermediate values by key and route them to the reduce workers.
apply the reduce function to each key's values to aggregate them into the final result.

limits: MapReduce is powerful but its model is deliberately restrictive, and several points reward care. Forcing every computation into a map-then-reduce shape is a poor fit for some problems, especially iterative algorithms like many in machine learning and graph processing, which must run many rounds and, in classic MapReduce, pay to write intermediate results to disk between each round; this inefficiency is exactly what later in-memory systems like Apache Spark addressed, largely superseding MapReduce for such workloads. MapReduce is batch-oriented, processing large datasets in bulk rather than in real time, so it does not suit low-latency or streaming needs. The programming model, though simple, can make some computations awkward to express, requiring them to be contorted into maps and reduces or chained across multiple jobs. Its fault tolerance depends on tasks being deterministic and re-runnable. Some historical details reward care: MapReduce is a model and implementation developed at Google, described by Dean and Ghemawat in 2004 at OSDI, popularized in open source by Apache Hadoop, and inspired by but not identical to functional programming's map and reduce; a later reprint appeared in 2008, but 2004 is the origin. So MapReduce robustly parallelizes big-data batch processing, understood as a restrictive, batch-oriented model less suited to iterative or real-time work, for which newer systems are preferred.
misreadings: MapReduce is not a general parallel-programming tool; its rigid map-then-reduce shape fits batch aggregation, not iterative or streaming work. It is not real-time, being batch-oriented. And it is inspired by, not identical to, functional map and reduce, so treating MapReduce as suiting every parallel task, as low-latency, or as the same as the functional combinators, misreads it.
origin: The programming model and implementation for parallel big-data processing developed at Google and described by Dean and Ghemawat in 2004, expressing computation as a map function and a reduce function run across a cluster.
